stories.topic: Joni Mitchell, Polio, and Fifty Alternative Tunings
stories.summary: At nine, Joni Mitchell got polio, which left her left hand much weaker for a long time. Instead of dropping the guitar, she invented about fifty alternative tunings. When she heard a chord in her head that she could not finger the standard way, she kept retuning the strings until the guitar produced it. David Crosby said her experiments blew his mind. She called the odd chords she found 'chords of inquiry,' and heard a whole orchestra in six strings, with the top three acting like a horn section. She later said polio gave her an inner life and made her an artist.
stories.insight: Because she couldn't play the guitar the normal way, she came to know it more closely than conventionally trained players did. Her distinct sound, which is hard to file under folk, blues or jazz, follows from that handicap. The constraint was no blessing for her, but it was a blessing for music.
stories.quote: It made me have an inner life and it turned me into an artist.

stories.topic: Shivani Wrote in the Middle of Family Dinner
stories.summary: Mrinal Pande told Amit how her mother, the Hindi writer Shivani, worked. She cooked, served the whole family, and then sat down and wrote while everyone ate and the children squabbled around her. She never waited for a vacation, a quiet retreat or an early-morning hour. The family simply learned not to disturb her. Amit tells this story to his writing students, especially women carrying a double load, when they say they have no time.
stories.insight: You don't have to remove your constraints before you start the work. Shivani worked in the scraps of time her life allowed. 'I'm too busy' is usually a story we tell ourselves.
stories.quote: And whatever little scraps of time I get within that, I will just sit and write.

stories.topic: Frida Kahlo Painting From Her Bed With a Mirror
stories.summary: Frida Kahlo had polio at six, which left one leg weaker and kept her out of school for months. At eighteen, on her way to becoming a doctor, she was in a wooden bus that collided with a rail car. A metal railing went through her pelvis and damaged her spine. She faced some thirty-two surgeries and long spells in bed. Her parents rigged an easel over her bed and placed a mirror so she could see herself, and her famous self-portraits followed. She also painted her plaster corsets and medical equipment. 'The Broken Column' (1944) came after a spinal surgery went wrong.
stories.insight: Her signature subject, herself, came partly from a bed, a mirror and forced solitude. She turned the tools of her confinement into her material and still lived a full life, including a stormy marriage to Diego Rivera.
stories.quote: I paint self portraits because I am so often alone, because I am the person I know best.

stories.topic: One Tennis Ball Among Twenty Kids
stories.summary: Ajay compares today's upper-class Indian children with his own childhood. Today's kids get rooms full of toys, tire of each one in three days and move on to the next. In his time, twenty children might share a single tennis ball and had to invent a whole day of fun using stones, trees and shrubs.
stories.insight: Scarcity makes the imagination work, and abundance can turn play into a treadmill of novelty.
stories.quote: There was like one tennis ball in a group of twenty people and everybody's intelligence and imagination and creativity had to be challenged on using stones and trees and shrubs and that one tennis ball to do fun things all day.

stories.topic: Gavaskar's Ground Strokes Were Built by Windows
stories.summary: Amit says, from memory, that Sunil Gavaskar's habit of keeping the ball along the ground came from gully cricket. If you broke a window, your ball or bat was confiscated and the game ended. Gavaskar rarely lofted the ball, a notable exception being his hundred against New Zealand in the 1987 World Cup.
stories.insight: A technique that looks like pure talent can be the trace of local rules from childhood play. The constraint coached him before any coach did.
stories.quote: So out of that constraint that I can't break any of these windows, he learned correct technique and how to play the ball along the ground.

stories.topic: Dr Seuss and the Fifty-Word Bet
stories.summary: Bennett Cerf, a co-founder of Random House and Dr Seuss's publisher, challenged Theodor Geisel to write a whole book using only fifty different words. The book could be any length, but its vocabulary had to stay within fifty words. Geisel reportedly kept a chart to track his words and pulled it off with Green Eggs and Ham. Amit read passages aloud ('I do not like green eggs and ham, I do not like them, Sam I am') to show how delightful the result is.
stories.insight: An arbitrary limit from outside produced a beloved classic. Amit uses the story to tell his writing students that a small vocabulary need not hold them back.
stories.quote: The idea was you have to write a full book using only fifty words.

stories.topic: Agatha Christie's Struggle With Words Became Her Style
stories.summary: Agatha Christie had dysgraphia and possibly dyslexia. She didn't give up writing. She developed a clear, concise prose style and very tight, intricate plotting that left no room for confusion.
stories.insight: A limitation, worked with honestly, can become the defining strength of a body of work.
stories.quote: So in a sense, out of that limitation arises a style that is a feature, not a bug.

stories.topic: Hemingway's Iceberg Came Out of the Newsroom
stories.summary: Hemingway's spare prose came partly from journalism, where he filed dispatches on deadline with no time for padding or polished sentences. From that economy grew his 'iceberg' approach. Only about an eighth of what is going on needs to appear on the page, and the rest lies underneath for the reader to infer. Amit adds that the famous six-word story 'For sale, baby shoes, never worn' is wrongly credited to Hemingway, who was six when it was first published.
stories.insight: Deadline pressure taught him economy, and economy became his style. Saying less leaves room for the reader to do some of the work.
stories.quote: Hemingway's point was that only one eighth needs to be in my story of what is really going on. And the rest can be undercurrent.

stories.topic: Dick Fosbury Couldn't Do the Straddle
stories.summary: In high school Dick Fosbury was bad at the standard high-jump technique, the straddle, in which you face the bar and cross it one leg at a time. He didn't have the coordination for it, so he experimented and was mocked like any heretic. Headlines said 'Fosbury flops,' likening him to a fish flopping into a boat. In 1968 he won Olympic gold with the Fosbury flop, which became the standard technique. Its spread also depended on deep foam landing mats replacing sand and shallow padding, which had made back-first landings dangerous. Amit admits he tried the high jump in school, failed and gave up.
stories.insight: Fosbury didn't reason his way to the flop from aerodynamics. He couldn't do the accepted method, so he found another one. And it took a second change, the removal of the hard-landing constraint, for his idea to succeed.
stories.quote: He had a constraint. He simply couldn't do the straddle. So he said, Okay, I will fight the constraint, and I will try some other way, and this happened to be the way that worked, and changed the sport completely.

stories.topic: Sachin's Double Hundred Without the Off Side
stories.summary: Sachin Tendulkar's tennis elbow, which he never fully disclosed, got so bad that, according to a close mutual friend, he couldn't lift a cup of tea. With a Test against Australia in Sydney ahead and no cover drive available to him, he chose to give up driving through the off side altogether. He made a double hundred without driving through the off side once.
stories.insight: Amit grants this isn't an innovation story like the others. It is about the best batsman in the world refusing to sit out, removing his favourite shot and still dominating.
stories.quote: And he makes a double hundred without driving through the offside even once.

stories.topic: Hacking Digger With a Broken Right Arm
stories.summary: At IIT, the big obsession among students was the keyboard game Digger, whose high scores were stored encrypted on a floppy disk and decided bragging rights. Ajay suffered multiple compound fractures of his right arm and couldn't play. With time on his hands, he disassembled the game's binary and studied it for hours. He found where each level's floor plan was stored and wrote an editor to design his own levels. He then built a level where the monsters died on their own, left the machine running overnight, and came back with 300,000 points against champions' 10,000 to 20,000.
stories.insight: Shut out of playing the game, he went one level up and rewrote it. Amit calls it cheating. Ajay notes it was the only time in his life he read binary, which he did only because the constraint left him nothing else to do.
stories.quote: And the world champions at the time had like scores of ten, twenty thousand and I re-emerged from my fractured right arm days with a high score of three hundred thousand.

stories.summary: In his IIT days, Ajay and his friends made hikes deliberately harder. They wore rubber chappals instead of shoes, carried very heavy loads, hiked at night, and eventually did all three at once.
stories.insight: Constraints you choose can turn something merely doable into something that fully engages your mind, much like playing chess blindfold.
stories.quote: So a night hike with a heavy load with rubber chappals. Just you know, load on the challenge and it comes to life.

stories.topic: A Failed Super-Glue Became the Post-it Note
stories.summary: Spencer Silver at 3M set out to create the strongest adhesive possible and failed. One attempt produced a notably weak adhesive, and using it gave him the idea that became the Post-it note. Post-its are now so common in offices that software imitates them with virtual versions.
stories.insight: A failure judged against the original goal can be a success against a different one.
stories.quote: And in fact one of his attempts is a spectacular failure because it is really a weak adhesive. But that weak adhesive when he uses it, it gives him an idea.

stories.summary: Coco Chanel came from a modest family and couldn't afford the silks and brocades of high fashion. So she experimented with cheaper fabrics such as jersey, then used for men's underwear, and made classy women's clothes from them. This also made her garments cheaper and more accessible.
stories.insight: A personal budget constraint started something that later became common in fashion. Lacking expensive materials pushed her toward a new kind of elegance that more people could afford.
stories.quote: I can't do high fashion with silks and brocades, but I can do beautiful couture with, you know, other garments and bring them to the fore.

stories.summary: In the early 1980s Keith Haring was an art student in New York who preferred painting in public to selling elitist gallery pieces. Expired subway advertisements were covered with black canvas, which made a ready-made surface. He had to work fast before the transit police arrived, so he used chalk. That speed, the medium and the knowledge that the work would soon disappear shaped a style of quick, iconic motifs, such as his barking dog. He later became famous and was commissioned for permanent murals, but the style stayed.
stories.insight: Having to hurry acted as a design brief. The conditions of illicit, fast public drawing produced a visual vocabulary that later became iconic.
stories.quote: Hey man, I gotta hurry and I just gotta get the job done, and chalk is the only thing that is suitable to what I'm trying to do.

recommendations.creator: Joni Mitchell
recommendations.context: Amit's opening story about Joni Mitchell. He first recommended the album in the Inflation Targeting episode.
recommendations.reason: Her unusual polio-driven approach to the guitar gives her a sound that fits no single genre. He says to listen to everything she made, starting with Blue, and singles out 'All I Want', 'Little Green', 'River' and 'A Case of You', which he also loves for her piano.

recommendations.creator: Dr Seuss
recommendations.context: Amit read passages aloud as a quiz for Ajay, then told the story of Bennett Cerf's fifty-word challenge.
recommendations.reason: It shows a tight constraint producing something joyful, and it supports his advice that writers don't need a big vocabulary.

recommendations.creator: Sara Rai
recommendations.context: Mentioned with his Seen and the Unseen episode with Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand's granddaughter.
recommendations.reason: He calls her a brilliant writer and this a great book of essays.

recommendations.item: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Brought up while discussing how a childhood without phones or the internet forced people to spend time with themselves.
recommendations.reason: Her childhood memories in the episode are vividly detailed, which he takes as an example of how close attention grows when you have nothing to distract you.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (Episode 263, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Source of the story about her mother Shivani writing amid family dinners.
recommendations.reason: A first-hand portrait of a legendary Hindi writer who wrote within the constraints of running a household.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Ira Pande (Episode 369, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned as his episode with Shivani's other daughter.
recommendations.reason: Another first-hand view of Shivani and her family.

recommendations.item: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned as his episode with Shivani's nephew, who was like a son to her.
recommendations.reason: Completes the set of conversations with the people closest to Shivani.

recommendations.item: Life's Grandeur: The Spread of Excellence From Plato to Darwin
recommendations.creator: Stephen Jay Gould
recommendations.context: While explaining that a sport's rules are its constraints, Amit recalled a book he read some thirty years ago but couldn't name. The show notes identify it.
recommendations.reason: He calls it brilliant on how baseball keeps adjusting its rules to keep the game balanced. That is a kind of central planning that works only because a game, unlike the real world, has bounded complexity.

recommendations.item: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when Amit noted that every instrument and form is a constraint. Ajay linked this to Amit's general theory of form.
recommendations.reason: It is the companion episode on how form shapes content, the larger frame this episode's constraint stories fit into.

recommendations.item: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the episode where he first recommended Joni Mitchell's Blue. Vaishnav Vyas calls it the 'inflammation targeting episode.'
recommendations.reason: It is where the Joni Mitchell recommendation first appeared, and it is linked in the show notes.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit referred to his online writing course, which has had more than 2,800 students, several times. He described its closing exercise of writing with no adverbs, no adjectives and no word over two syllables.
recommendations.reason: The course uses deliberate constraints to make students look closely at their sentences and the words they choose.

core_ideas.explanation: The brain can't take in the world's full complexity. So we tell stories that are simpler than reality, never entirely true, but useful, and our creativity grows out of that limit. Ajay points out that a storyteller's 'story' and a scientist's 'model' are the same thing, as in George Box's line that all models are wrong but some are useful.
core_ideas.quote: We are both creative because we are both stupid.

core_ideas.explanation: This is the episode's thesis. A disability, poverty, a deadline, a word limit or a publisher's challenge doesn't only reduce what you can do. It sends effort in directions an unconstrained person would never try, as with Joni Mitchell's tunings, Frida Kahlo's self-portraits, the Fosbury flop and Chanel's jersey. Amit stresses that the constraint isn't good in itself, polio least of all. The value lies in how people respond to it.
core_ideas.quote: It's a blessing to music because it pushed a person, forced a person into going into different directions and doing interesting things.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay separates constraints the world forces on you, such as polio or a broken arm, from constraints you choose, such as blindfold chess, hiking at night in chappals, writing without adverbs, or Apple setting thinness and weight targets for the MacBook Air that existing technology couldn't meet. Chosen constraints can be just a game, but often they wake the mind up and push invention.
core_ideas.quote: It's like the constraint is what brings it to life.

core_ideas.concept: Everything Is Constrained, Everything Is Boundless
core_ideas.explanation: Every form is a constraint, whether a guitar, a keyboard, an 800-word column, a 280-character tweet, a 60–90 minute show or the rules of a sport. Fielding restrictions in one-day cricket and the offside rule in football change incentives and so change the game. Someone who loves a form, like Eddie Van Halen with the guitar, sees possibilities rather than limits.
core_ideas.quote: So actually everything is constrained and everything is boundless opportunity. And the question is how do you look at it?

core_ideas.explanation: Writers worry that their vocabulary is too small. Amit argues that a writer never needs more words than the readers know, since the goal is to be understood. Reading widely will expand your vocabulary, but what limits good writing is care, not word count.
core_ideas.quote: I do not believe, Ajay Shah, that any writer needs a greater vocabulary than her readers.

core_ideas.explanation: Hemingway's iceberg idea says to put only a fraction of what is happening on the page and let the reader infer the rest from small cues, like an impatient look or a tapping finger. Economy here means trusting the reader, not leaving things out.
core_ideas.quote: It is not only show don't tell, but it is show enough and no more.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit used to complain about 800-word column limits, write 1,200 words, and then find that what he cut wasn't needed. Deadlines force work to get finished. Haiku (5-7-5 syllables) and his no-adverb, no-adjective, no-long-word exercise make writers look closely at language. Great lyricists like Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar always wrote to meter and music.
core_ideas.quote: You need that artificial constraint to get it done.

core_ideas.concept: A Constraint Triggers an Innovation; Removing One Lets It Spread
core_ideas.explanation: Fosbury invented the flop because he couldn't do the straddle. The flop took over only because deep foam mats made landing on your back safe. New ideas often need something pushing them into being and an old barrier being lifted.
core_ideas.quote: The Fosbury flop might have been incentivized by a constraint. But the success of it was incentivized by the removal of a constraint.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that mathematically, adding constraints to an optimisation problem can at best match the unconstrained optimum and usually does worse. The stories in this episode go the other way because humans don't accept the problem as given. They rethink the objective and the framing, which a solver cannot do.
core_ideas.quote: If you respect the frame, then it's inevitable that as you layer on the constraints, it gets worse.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cautions that millions of people got polio and for most it made life worse. We remember the few who broke through. Be inspired by them, but don't mistake the exceptions for the typical outcome.
core_ideas.quote: Millions of people were struck down by polio. On average it was a bad thing for their lives.

core_ideas.explanation: New technology borrows the look of what it replaces so people feel at home: an e-book app drawn as a bookshelf, a floppy-disk save icon, folder icons, virtual Post-its. Ajay adds that a phone camera's 'pro' mode shows aperture and exposure controls, but it is all image processing and nothing physical changes. The shutter click is a fake sound too. The approach helps early adoption but can outlast its usefulness.
core_ideas.quote: They're just exploiting your views of user interface to a device that has nothing to do with that world.

core_ideas.concept: The Lost Constraint of Having Nothing to Do
core_ideas.explanation: Amit and Ajay grew up without the internet or mobile phones and had to spend time with themselves. That is how Frida Kahlo's solitude and Sara Rai's richly observed childhood came about. Amit wonders whether losing boredom has turned us into creatures that hop from one stimulus to the next and rarely spend time with ourselves.
core_ideas.quote: I wonder in modern times if the absence of the constraint called nothing to do has made us into creatures who are going from sensation to sensation and not spending enough time with ourselves.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens offended at being called stupid, saying that in any decent age he would have slapped Amit with a glove and fought a duel at fifty paces 'with rusty guns that barely aim accurately.' Amit, the libertarian, replies: 'So much talk about the coercion of the state, monopoly on violence. Are you the state that you can threaten me with violence?'
Amit refuses to 'tell us about models': 'None of the people I'm talking about today is a model per se in the fashion model sense, but they are all models for us to aspire to.'

Amit accuses Ajay of hijacking his recommendation of Derek and the Dominos' 'Layla' the previous week: 'quite creative, anything but stupid, but deeply devious.' He also notes that Vaishnav Vyas calls the Inflation Targeting episode 'the inflammation targeting episode.'
On Frida Kahlo's supportive parents: 'God bless their souls, though we don't believe in God, but flying spaghetti monster should bless their souls.'

Showing viewers a Dr Seuss page that Ajay can't see, Amit compares it to a chess broadcast, where everyone sees the engine evaluation except the two players: 'So they are the two chutiyas who don't know the right move. Everybody else does.'
Amit describes Spencer Silver's quest for the strongest adhesive known to man as trying to make 'Fevikwik ka baap.'
Amit on cricket: 'every good Indian by the definition of that for the purpose of this chapter is someone who follows cricket,' which rules out Ajay, who doesn't.

On the Digger saga, Amit first asks of the 'most important male objective' at IIT: 'What kind of male objective is that? Shame on you.' When Ajay mentions breaking his right hand, Amit adds a family-show aside that 'it's much better for a male engineer to injure his right hand than his left hand.' Then: 'At one level this might be called adapting to constraints. Fancy term. This is cheating.' Finally: 'Nomsita, leave this in... let the world see what a shameless man this is... at one level I just lost respect for you, but at another level I gained respect for you.'
Amit calls Everything is Everything a work of art made within a 60–90 minute limit: 'Aren't you still watching? If you're still watching, you can't diss.'

Picking up Ajay's phrase 'black and white fact,' Amit says, 'It should be noted that I am right now a black and white fact.' He then reminds Ajay that he promised five recommendations for this episode. When Ajay tries to defer, Amit threatens to demand ten, and they settle on six for the next episode.
George Box's line 'All models are wrong, some models are useful,' quoted by Ajay to argue that stories and scientific models are the same thing.
Douglas Adams: 'I love deadlines, especially the sound they make as they go whooshing by,' quoted by Amit on deadlines as a constraint of time.
Frida Kahlo: 'Feet, what do I need you for when I have wings to fly.' Amit says it would sound cheesy if you didn't know who said it.
Joni Mitchell called herself 'a painter derailed by circumstance,' though she painted all her own album covers. Amit notes that 'Both Sides Now' is one of Ajay's favourite songs.
The six-word story 'For sale, baby shoes, never worn,' wrongly attributed to Hemingway, who was six years old when it was first published.

Examples of great writing under constraint: Shakespeare, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address ('in one sixty seven words or something'), and Hindi film lyricists Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar writing to meter and music.
Eddie Van Halen playing 'Eruption' and sometimes switching to the piano, used to show that every instrument is both a constraint and a set of possibilities.
Gavaskar's 1987 World Cup hundred against New Zealand, 'hitting even Chatfield all over the park,' the rare time he lofted the ball.
